name: Bluetip
label: Dischord
lede: Two Swiz alumni, a name lifted off a box of kitchen matches, five drummers in six years, and a last record that named the band that came next.

eras.title: Swiz kids strike again
eras.text: Swiz had been one of the most popular bands in DC's younger hardcore scene of the late '80s, Dischord says. Five years after it ended, Jason Farrell and Dave Stern started over with a heavier, more rock band and put it straight onto the road.

years.p: [[Jason Farrell|f458f662-c72b-485b-9152-81eda8659fdb]] and [[Dave Stern|636e5c15-b268-404f-8e01-6240caecc53c]] of [[Swiz|eea2f3d8-1e94-436c-ae66-4633f99f55be]] reunite with bassist [[Jake Kump|037cdc96-518b-48f4-81bf-3cf095f0de54]] and drummer Zac Eller of Worlds Collide. At first they're called The Ohio Blue Tip, like the matches.
years.xp:
Swiz ran from 1987 to 1990, with Jason Farrell on guitar and Dave Stern joining on bass at the end. Wikipedia says the new band started out as The Ohio Blue Tip before trimming it to Bluetip.

AllMusic hears [[Fugazi|233fc3f3-6de2-465c-985e-e721dbabbace]], [[Killing Joke|f5aca88c-e3c1-4bc2-af33-68a9a9f7b56a]] and [[Mission of Burma|db9d25d7-a85b-4a29-b2ff-8f5b69ed691e]] in the result. Dischord describes a band with an intense work schedule from the start.

years.h: Bluetip's debut, Dischord No. 101, named for its catalog number
years.p: Bluetip's debut, produced by [[Ian MacKaye|c12f644b-1066-4ead-b0dd-d0c380f5cca2]] at Inner Ear Studios. A Dischord reviewer called it one of the label's most rock 'n' roll releases.
years.xp: [[Don Zientara|a495882b-4585-4295-9269-e30c63f279fe]] engineered. Thirteen songs, opening with one called "Nickelback."

years.p: Wikipedia credits Bluetip's early reputation to tours with Tool, the Melvins and Hoover. Not the usual company for a Dischord band.

years.h: Bluetip's first drummer, Zac Eller, leaves
years.p: Eller leaves after the debut album. Wikipedia lists [[Joe Gorelick|cfc54588-c9b2-4417-bfd8-4a7e4509af3f]] filling in during 1996, then [[Aaron Ford|2e5fcee9-c0bd-4a92-82d1-f76b924b758a]] taking the seat.

years.h: Live at Extreme Noise Records, Minneapolis, May 27, 1996
yt: Live at Extreme Noise Records, Minneapolis, May 27, 1996

eras.title: Join Us, and a revolving drum stool
eras.text: The second album brought in J. Robbins of Jawbox as producer and a sharper, tighter sound. Behind the kit, the band kept changing, and Dischord is frank that internal conflicts were part of why.

years.h: Jason Farrell and Dave Stern's side project, Sweetbelly Freakdown
years.p: The two Bluetip guitarists also run Sweetbelly Freakdown, which puts out material in 1997, per AllMusic.

years.h: Bluetip's Join Us, produced by J. Robbins
years.p: Recorded at Inner Ear with [[J. Robbins|3babd931-a940-43a8-b629-d7aed5b821d9]] of [[Jawbox|016fba14-1fc6-4986-86c2-2113ec9b28de]] producing and Aaron Ford on drums. Dischord also issued a two-song Join Us single from the same sessions.

years.h: Bluetip drummer Aaron Ford out, Dave Bryson in
years.p: Aaron Ford leaves and [[Dave Bryson|32151168-adcd-4245-8aba-d8c69a9456a1]] takes over the drums. Dischord's history says Bluetip's line-up changes came from internal conflicts.
years.xp:
By Wikipedia's count Bluetip went through five drummers: Eller, Gorelick, Ford, Bryson and, at the very end, Areif Dasha Sless-Kitain. Dischord's own shorter version says Eller left after the debut and Bryson replaced him, skipping the middle.

Wikipedia puts the band's eventual end down to creative differences.

eras.title: Polymer, Japan and a move to New York
eras.text: With Stern gone and Brian Clancy on second guitar, Bluetip made its most focused record and took it as far as Japan. Then Farrell moved to New York, and the band ended with him.

years.h: Dave Stern leaves Bluetip; Brian Clancy joins
years.p: Dave Stern leaves after Join Us. Brian Clancy takes over his guitar spot.
J. Robbins produces again, this time at Phase Studios, with the Jason Farrell, Brian Clancy, Jake Kump and Dave Bryson line-up. Eleven songs, including "Don't Punch Your Friend (for being slow)."

years.h: Bluetip tours the US, Europe and Japan
years.p: Dischord says Bluetip toured the US, Europe and Japan through its run. The final Bluetip record, P.M.A., has a song called "Japan" on it.
The final Bluetip record, pieced together from sessions at seven places, from WGNS and Inner Ear to a "Pirate house" and "My House." Track eight, "Retisonic," names Jason Farrell's next band.

years.h: Jason Farrell moves to New York, and Bluetip ends
years.p: Dischord's history is blunt: when Jason Farrell moved to New York in 2001, Bluetip folded. Its timeline runs to January 2002.

years.h: Live at the Temple, Dublin, April 17, 2001
yt: Live at the Temple, Dublin, April 17, 2001

eras.title: The song becomes a band
eras.text: Farrell took the name of a Bluetip song for his next band, kept designing record covers, and eventually got the Swiz guys back together under a new name.

years.p: Farrell's new band, named after a Bluetip song, releases the Lean Beat EP. Bluetip also turns up on the 20 Years of Dischord set, Dischord No. 125.
Wikipedia notes Bluetip got back together briefly in 2008. AllMusic dates the band's official end to the same year.

years.h: Jason Farrell and Dave Stern form [[Red Hare|8e5d7f42-eae5-4b5c-aa06-88b6066f0ea3]]
years.p: The two ex-Bluetip guitarists team up with Swiz singer [[Shawn Brown|e39556a4-0d8f-4138-bc18-a54d3a66eefe]]. Farrell, a working designer, has put his art on a long list of album covers.
